glance: Anthropic priced its IPO at a reported $83 a share, above its range, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion before trading starts on Nasdaq today. Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a cheaper mid-tier model, and Google Labs showed Stitch Loop, an agent that keeps improving live products and opens pull requests for fixes. Also: 59 European tech leaders ask the EU to fund AI properly, Siemens takes Simcenter X to Azure, Škoda's virtual homologation patent, Einride's autonomous truck numbers, and two new bearing papers.
brief: Here is Vertical News for Thursday the nineteenth of November. Anthropic priced its stock market debut on Wednesday at a reported eighty-three dollars a share, above its planned range. That values the company at about one and a half trillion dollars, and trading on Nasdaq under the ticker A N T begins today. Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a mid-tier model priced at three dollars per million input tokens, which Google says does tasks a third cheaper than its top model. Vercel added it to its AI Gateway the same day. Google Labs also showed Stitch Loop, an experimental agent that watches a live product, proposes fixes with design options, and opens pull requests that a person must approve. In Europe, fifty-nine tech leaders, including the heads of Lovable, DeepL and ElevenLabs, asked the EU to set aside real money for AI in its next long-term budget. Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute for four and a half billion dollars in stock. OpenAI says its models found up to fourteen percent better power, performance and area in AMD graphics chip blocks. Satya Nadella said most Microsoft staff will end up managing AI agents. Siemens will offer its Simcenter X simulation service on Microsoft Azure. Škoda has patented a way to approve speed assistance largely through virtual tests. Boston Dynamics will expand Spot robots at GlobalFoundries, which will also test Atlas. Einride reported growing driverless hours, and Hongqi is looking for a European factory. Two new papers cover gas foil bearings and bearing fault diagnosis under heavy noise.

stories.headline: Anthropic prices its IPO at a reported $83 a share, valuing it at about $1.5 trillion
stories.why: The first frontier AI lab to go public sets a market price on the models many product teams now build on.
body: Anthropic priced its initial public offering on Wednesday evening at $83 a share, according to TechCrunch, above the $70–78 range it had marketed to investors. At that price the company is valued at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from $965 billion at its last private round in May. CNBC reported that the offering raised more than $81 billion, making it the largest IPO on record. Shares start trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT today.

Alongside the IPO, a group of strategic investors including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting shares in a private placement. Amazon owns nearly 15% of the company and Google almost 14%. According to the S-1, each of the seven co-founders sold just under 3.4 million shares, worth about $282 million each.

For teams that depend on Claude, a listed Anthropic will publish quarterly results, giving more visibility into pricing, capacity and priorities. The pricing came despite a nervous week for AI stocks after Nvidia's leadership change.

stories.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon, a mid-tier model at $3 per million input tokens
stories.why: A strong coding model at a middle price gives frontend and product teams another option to test on cost per task.
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon, which sits between Gemini 4 Carbon, its model for the hardest long-running work, and Hydrogen, the fast everyday model launched last week. Neon has a one-million-token context window and four thinking levels. API pricing is $3 per million input tokens, $15 per million output tokens and $0.15 per million cached input tokens. Google says a typical task costs 32% less than with Carbon at the default setting.

Google's own benchmark figures put Neon first on Artificial Analysis's coding agent index and second on the Vals Index, with 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1. It is available in the paid Gemini API, Gemini for business, Antigravity and the Gemini app for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Vercel added it to its AI Gateway on the same day, with tool calling and structured outputs.

With GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and now Neon all released within a week, teams have several mid-priced models to compare on their own tasks. Google has not said whether there are any regional limits in Europe.

stories.headline: Google Labs launches Stitch Loop, an agent that keeps improving live products and opens pull requests for fixes
stories.why: Design tools are moving from drawing screens to improving shipped products against real metrics, with accessibility built in.
body: Google Labs introduced Stitch Loop, an experimental, long-running product agent in its Stitch design family. It connects to a team's GitHub repository and to live product data such as logs, user behaviour and feedback, using more than 180 integrations, custom MCP servers and command-line uploads.

Each loop finds problems backed by evidence, proposes solutions with trade-offs and visual design options, builds the chosen fix in a cloud sandbox and opens a GitHub pull request with screenshots and video. It then watches live metrics to see whether the change worked. Three loops come by default: security (using Gemini 4 Carbon and DeepMind's CodeMender), latency and accessibility. Teams can add their own goals, such as checkout conversion. Nothing is merged without human review, and a Slack integration sends daily digests. There is a global waitlist, with AI Ultra subscribers first, and no pricing yet.
For designers, this moves AI from the mock-up stage into the live product. The accessibility loop is relevant to European teams now working under the European Accessibility Act.

stories.headline: 59 European tech leaders, including the heads of Lovable, DeepL and ElevenLabs, urge the EU to fund AI in its 2028–34 budget
stories.why: Europe's next long-term budget will decide how much public money backs European AI companies into the 2030s.
body: An open letter signed by 59 founders, investors and researchers from all 27 member states asks EU leaders to treat AI as a budget priority. Signatories include Yann LeCun of AMI Labs, economist Philippe Aghion, the chief executives of ElevenLabs, Lovable and DeepL, OVHcloud's Octave Klaba and researchers Sepp Hochreiter and Bernhard Schölkopf.

The letter welcomes the first Digital Omnibus but says simplification must go further, including a real EU-wide company regime and consistent rules for employee stock options. It asks for pension and insurance savings to flow into scale-up funds, governments to act as first customers, a dedicated AI line in the European Competitiveness Fund and the next research programme, and annual reviews of AI targets by heads of government. It warns that anything left out of the 2028–34 budget will not exist before 2035.

The Next Web notes that several signatories would benefit directly from what they ask for. For European product teams, the letter shows where the political debate is heading as the AI Act takes effect.

stories.headline: Palo Alto Networks agrees to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock
stories.why: Security vendors are betting that companies will fine-tune and run their own open-weight models, and need to secure them.
stories.source: Palo Alto Networks (SEC filing) · AI Weekly
body: Palo Alto Networks signed a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute in an all-stock deal worth about $4.5 billion, subject to adjustments. The deal is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks' fiscal third quarter of 2027, pending regulatory approval. Applied Compute runs a platform for post-training and inference that lets companies adapt open-weight models to their own data and run them, and it will keep serving its customers.

Applied Compute's chief executive and co-founder Yash Patil will become a co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks. According to AI Weekly, citing the Wall Street Journal, the start-up was founded in 2025 by three former OpenAI staff and was valued at $3.25 billion when it raised $350 million at the start of November.

The deal shows that customised, in-house models are becoming a security and governance question. Teams that fine-tune open models on company data should expect more tooling, and more scrutiny, around that work.

stories.headline: Nadella says most Microsoft employees will become managers of AI agents
stories.why: It is a clear signal of how a large software company plans to reorganise product and engineering teams around agents.
body: Speaking at the DealBook Summit, Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella explained why the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees in October instead of another round of layoffs. He said AI is the driver, but described the change as a reorganisation around directing AI rather than simply replacing engineers, and said the buyouts give staff more control over their choices.

As an example he pointed to the team behind Cowork, Microsoft's agent in Microsoft 365: 11 developers who build a 'software factory' that in turn produces the product. He predicted that most employees will end up managing AI agents, but said Microsoft, at 51 years old, was not built AI-first, so the change will take longer than people expect.

For product leaders, the comments add to growing evidence that team structures, roles and hiring are being redesigned around agents. The skills that matter shift towards specifying, reviewing and steering automated work.

stories.headline: OpenAI says its models found up to 14% gains in power, performance and area on AMD GPU designs
stories.why: It is a concrete example of AI improving mature engineering designs that experts had already optimised.
body: OpenAI reported that its models rewrote SystemVerilog code for selected blocks of AMD's flagship GPU designs and found up to 14% improvement in power, performance and area on circuits AMD had already tuned for years. Synopsys tools checked that each rewrite behaved the same as the original and measured the trade-offs. AMD separately reported single-digit gains on a next-generation CPU.

OpenAI also said that on its own first inference chip, called Jalapeño, AI-assisted design cut area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit in silicon, with nine months from design start to tape-out. OpenAI admits its models sometimes dropped features that were in the original designs. The AMD figures come from OpenAI's own reporting.

For engineering teams, the pattern matters more than the chip: AI proposes changes, and established verification tools prove them equivalent. The same split between generation and formal checking is relevant wherever simulation and sign-off tools already exist.

stories.headline: Siemens will offer its Simcenter X simulation service on Microsoft Azure
stories.why: Cloud access to Siemens' simulation suite could make high-performance CAE easier to scale for OEMs and suppliers already on Azure.
body: Siemens announced that Simcenter X, its software-as-a-service suite for multi-domain simulation, will be offered on Microsoft Azure and through Microsoft Marketplace. Simcenter X combines simulation apps, AI tools and high-performance computing. Siemens did not give a launch date.

Siemens' Teamcenter X, Designcenter X and Polarion X already run on Azure, so the move puts simulation alongside PLM, design and requirements tools on the same cloud. The plan is being shown at Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco this week. The two companies have worked together for more than 35 years.

For simulation teams in automotive, the practical question is whether solver licences, data and compute can sit in the same cloud tenant as product data, which would simplify traceability between requirements, models and results. Pricing and regional availability have not been announced.

stories.headline: Škoda patents 'virtually assisted homologation' for its speed assistance system
stories.why: It shows how virtual testing, checked by an independent body, is already being used for EU type approval of ADAS functions.
body: Škoda has applied for a patent on a method that approves Intelligent Speed Assistance, which every new car registered in the EU must have, largely through virtual and lab tests. Three of the four required test types are done in simulation or on the bench. The fourth is a physical drive over 400 km of roads chosen by an independent organisation, used to confirm the simulation results.

The method was developed with Škoda's subsidiary Digiteq Automotive, and TÜV SÜD Czech assessed how reliable the virtual testing is. The patent application rests on about 400 pages of documentation. The current Peaq, Enyaq and Elroq were the first models approved this way. Škoda says it saves dozens or even hundreds of weeks of road testing each year.

For validation engineers, this is a working example of the model that UNECE and EU rules are moving towards: simulation does most of the work, and a smaller set of physical tests confirms that the model is credible.

stories.headline: Boston Dynamics expands Spot inspections at GlobalFoundries, which will test the Atlas humanoid from 2027
stories.why: Inspection robots in chip fabs show what autonomous condition monitoring can do in a demanding production setting.
stories.source: Robotics & Automation News · Design Development Today
body: GlobalFoundries will use Boston Dynamics' Spot robot for autonomous asset inspection at its fabs in Malta, New York, Burlington, Vermont, Dresden and Singapore. Spot has been running in Burlington for more than four years. In Singapore, two robots have covered nearly 900 km since April and completed more than 90,000 sub-fab inspections with a 99% mission success rate.

GlobalFoundries moved 875 routine inspections to Spot in two weeks and plans to more than double that. It will also be the first customer outside the car industry to test the Atlas humanoid, through an early-adopter programme, with on-site testing from early 2027.

For factories and test labs, the numbers are a useful benchmark for robotic inspection rounds that collect thermal, acoustic and visual data, and for the shift from reactive to predictive maintenance.

stories.headline: Einride reports 8,500 driverless hours and 27% revenue growth in its third quarter
stories.why: The Swedish company's numbers give rare real-world data on Level 4 trucks operating under European permits.
body: Swedish freight technology company Einride reported third-quarter revenue of SEK 185.9 million, up 27% on the second quarter, and contracted annual recurring revenue of about $167 million, up 76% since June. It has more than 40 customers, more than 260 electric trucks and 10 autonomous trucks. Driverless hours in contracted operations rose from about 5,400 in June to about 8,500 by 13 November.

Einride holds driverless permits in four countries and five US states. A cab-less Level 4 truck has been running on a public road in Germany with Lidl since September under a KBA permit, and highway autonomy is targeted from the first half of 2028. Its next-generation driving system is being built on Nvidia's Hyperion platform. Cash fell to SEK 533 million, and the company widened its second-half loss guidance; it targets cash-flow breakeven in 2028.
For engineers working on autonomy and type approval, the German permit is the most interesting detail: it shows how a driverless vehicle without a cab is being approved for public roads in Europe.

stories.headline: Hongqi looks for a European factory and names Stellantis and VW as possible partners
stories.why: More Chinese brands want to build in Europe, which affects plant use, platform sharing and local sourcing for suppliers.
body: FAW's international chief Xiao Xiao told Reuters at the European launch of the Hongqi EHS4 in Venice that building cars in Europe is a strategic priority. He said Stellantis is not the only possible partner and pointed to FAW's long relationship with Volkswagen in China. Volkswagen Group China said there are no talks with FAW about building cars in Europe.

Reuters had earlier reported talks about a Stellantis plant in Spain, where Stellantis already builds cars with Leapmotor. Hongqi prefers to use existing European plants rather than build its own. The EHS4 uses a Leapmotor platform and starts at €32,900 as a battery-electric car, with a range-extender version due in 2027. Hongqi sells in 27 European markets through 90 dealers and plans 10 models in Europe in 2027.
For European suppliers, local production by Chinese brands means new sourcing decisions, and more pressure on under-used European plants to find partners.

stories.headline: Study shows a two-pad gas foil bearing nearly matches the load capacity of a one-pad design, with better stability
stories.why: Oil-free foil bearings matter for e-compressors and fuel-cell air supply in electric vehicles.
body: Researchers at Wuxi Taihu University and Beijing Institute of Technology compared gas foil journal bearings with one, two and three pads of the same size and without preload. They used a compressible Reynolds equation for the gas film, coupled to a detailed model of the foil structure, and checked it against published film-thickness data. The peer-reviewed paper was published in Lubricants on 18 November.

The two-pad bearing carried almost as much load as the one-pad design and clearly more than the three-pad design. Because the pad joints sit horizontally, stiffness differs by direction, which raised the predicted stability margin of a rigid rotor. A longer lower pad added horizontal stiffness with little loss of load capacity. An uneven pad layout worked best at light loads and an even layout at moderate loads.

For designers of high-speed electric compressors and turbo machines, the results suggest a two-pad layout can improve rotor stability without giving up much load capacity. The results are simulation-based; the abstract gives no test-rig numbers.

stories.headline: Weighting sensors by how reliable they look helps bearing fault diagnosis stay accurate in heavy noise
stories.why: Condition monitoring in real vehicles and plants has to cope with noisy, partly faulty sensors.
stories.source: Journal of Mechanical Science and Technology
body: A peer-reviewed study from Zhengzhou Business University, published online on 12 November, combines vibration, motor current, acoustic and temperature data to diagnose bearing faults. A separate autoencoder for each sensor learns what normal signals look like; how badly it reconstructs a new signal is used as a measure of how reliable that sensor is at that moment. A Transformer model then weights the sensors by those scores before classifying the fault.

The method reached 99.31% accuracy on an NSK 6205 bearing dataset and 99.67% on the public Paderborn dataset. With strong added noise, at a signal-to-noise ratio of minus 10 dB, it still reached 88.04% and 90.37%, which the authors say beats the comparison models. The weights also show which sensor drove each decision.
For condition-monitoring teams, the approach offers a way to keep diagnosis working when one sensor degrades. The tests use lab datasets, so field validation is still needed.

watch.title: Anthropic's first day of trading
watch.text: ANT starts trading on Nasdaq today after pricing above its range. The first-day move will show how public markets value frontier AI labs after a shaky week for AI stocks.

watch.text: The Information reports that Bret Taylor's customer-service agent company is in talks to raise about $1.5 billion, nearly doubling its May valuation. Not yet confirmed.

watch.text: Carmakers want leaders to delay the stricter EV rules of origin due on 1 January. Watch for any mention in the joint declaration.
